title: AI-Assisted Engineering and Code Review
description: Work with coding assistants as an engineer who owns the result: instructions and context, specs and tests first, small steps, reading and securing machine-written changes, and measuring the effect.
audience: A developer who can read Python and SQL and use git. The ai-engineering and ai-agents courses explain how models and agents work; this one is about using them and reviewing their output.
outcomes: You'll be able to write a specification and tests that an assistant's change must satisfy.
You'll be able to read a diff against its intent and find unrequested changes.
You'll be able to spot typical machine-made defects and security faults.
You'll be able to separate an assistant's claim from evidence.
You'll be able to write working rules and measure whether assistance helps.

modules.title: Working with a coding assistant
modules.summary: What an assistant is, how its context and instructions shape its output, and how specs, tests and small steps keep you in control.

modules.title: Reviewing machine-written code
modules.summary: How to read a diff for intent, recover your bearings in unfamiliar code, and find the defects and security faults assistants typically produce.

modules.title: Evidence and professional practice
modules.summary: Showing that a change works, owning the licensing and privacy consequences, and setting working rules that you measure.

lessons.title: What a coding assistant does and does not do
lessons.objective: Distinguish completion, chat and agentic assistants and state where responsibility for the change lies.

concepts.title: Assistant modes
concepts.summary: Inline completion, chat, and agentic editing in which the tool reads files, runs commands and edits.

concepts.title: Accountability
concepts.summary: The person who merges a change owns it, whatever wrote it.

concepts.title: Acceptance rate
concepts.summary: The share of suggested code kept unchanged.

misconceptions: The assistant knows the codebase; it sees only the files and text placed in its context.
If tests pass the change is right; tests describe what someone thought to check.
A suggestion is the assistant's responsibility; the reviewer who merges it owns it.
sequence: The same task, rename a function, done by completion, chat and an agentic tool.
What each mode can see and change.
Where mistakes enter: missing context, plausible code, unverified claims.
The owner of the change.

lessons.title: Context and instruction files
lessons.objective: Decide what to put in an assistant's context, write a project instruction file, and estimate whether a codebase fits in the window.

concepts.title: Context
concepts.summary: Everything the model sees on a call: instructions, files, history and tool results.

concepts.title: Instruction file
concepts.summary: A checked-in text file of commands, conventions and boundaries read at the start of each session.

concepts.title: Context pollution
concepts.summary: Stale, irrelevant or contradictory text in the context that degrades output.

misconceptions: Give the assistant the whole repository; relevant files in a small context beat everything in a huge one.
An instruction file is documentation for people; it is read by the model on every session and should hold only what changes its behaviour.
A long conversation is a better context than a fresh start; once it fills with dead ends, start again with a summary.
sequence: What the assistant can see on a task.
Estimating size: 40,000 lines at about 10 tokens a line.
What goes in an instruction file: build and test commands, conventions, forbidden actions.
Resetting context.
examples: 40,000 lines × 10 tokens = 400,000 tokens, against a 200,000-token window: half the codebase fits.
Good line: 'Run pnpm check before reporting done.' Weak line: 'Write clean code.'

lessons.title: Specification first
lessons.objective: Write a specification with testable acceptance criteria before asking an assistant to build.

concepts.title: Acceptance criteria
concepts.summary: Statements that a test can pass or fail.

concepts.title: Edge case
concepts.summary: Input at a boundary or outside the usual range where behaviour must be stated.

concepts.title: Non-goal
concepts.summary: Something the change must not do.

misconceptions: A detailed prompt is a spec; a spec says what is observably true afterwards, and prompts without it get a plausible guess.
Edge cases are the assistant's job to think of; it tends to implement the main case.
The spec is finished when the code is generated; the spec is the review checklist.
sequence: A function slugify(text) with a one-line request.
Rewriting the request as criteria, edge cases and non-goals.
Turning each criterion into a test input.
Using the spec as the review checklist.
examples: Criteria: lowercase; each run of non-alphanumeric characters becomes one hyphen; no leading or trailing hyphen; empty input returns ''. slugify('  Hello, World! ') is 'hello-world'; slugify('A  B--C') is 'a-b-c'.

figures.shows: Spec lines on the left, test cases generated from each on the right.
slugify stub and a list of asserts.

lessons.title: Tests as the contract
lessons.objective: Judge whether a test suite would catch a defect, using mutation score and assertions rather than line coverage.

concepts.title: Assertion
concepts.summary: A check inside a test that fails when behaviour is wrong.

concepts.title: Mutation score
concepts.summary: The share of deliberately injected faults that the tests detect.

concepts.title: Coverage
concepts.summary: The share of lines that run during tests, which says nothing about whether outputs are checked.

misconceptions: 100% coverage means the code is tested; code can run without anything being checked.
Letting the assistant write the tests for its own code proves the code does what it does.
If tests pass, a rule that passes the tests must be right; assistants sometimes special-case the tests.
sequence: is_leap(year) written as year % 4 == 0 and tests for 2024 and 2023 that pass.
Which input exposes the bug: 1900.
Mutation: change an operator and see whether any test fails.
Writing tests first, from the spec, then watching them fail.
examples: Century rule: divisible by 100 is not leap unless divisible by 400, so 1900 is not leap and 2000 is.
20 injected faults, 15 caught by tests: mutation score 15/20 = 75%.

lessons.title: Small steps and version control
lessons.objective: Split a large change into reviewable commits and use version control to checkpoint and undo.

concepts.title: Commit
concepts.summary: A recorded, reversible snapshot of a change.

concepts.title: Checkpoint
concepts.summary: A commit made before a risky step so that you can return to it.

concepts.title: Revert
concepts.summary: A new commit that undoes an earlier one without rewriting history.

misconceptions: A single big change is faster to review; large diffs get skimmed.
Reset and revert are the same; reset rewrites history and revert adds a commit, so only revert is safe on a shared branch.
The assistant will commit sensibly; you decide the boundaries.
sequence: A 1,200-line diff arrives at once.
Break the task into steps each with its own test and commit.
Checkpoint before letting an agent edit widely.
Undo options.
examples: 1,200 lines in steps of at most 300 gives 4 commits.
git reset --soft HEAD~1 undoes the last commit and keeps its changes staged; git revert <sha> adds a commit that reverses it.

lessons.title: Recovering your bearings in unfamiliar code
lessons.objective: Reconstruct the structure of a codebase from entry points, boundaries and dependencies, and verify an assistant's description of it.

concepts.title: Entry point
concepts.summary: Where execution starts, such as a main function or a route table.

concepts.title: Module boundary
concepts.summary: The line between parts that other parts reach only through an interface.

concepts.title: Claim check
concepts.summary: Confirming a statement about code by finding the line that makes it true.

misconceptions: The assistant's summary of the codebase is accurate; it can state a convincing structure that the code does not have.
Reading every file is the only way; reading entry points, boundaries, data access, errors and tests recovers most of the structure.
The file names tell you the architecture; names show intent and code shows behaviour.
sequence: A repository the assistant wrote quickly.
Find the entry points, then follow one request through.
Locate data access, auth, error handling, configuration and tests.
Check three claims from the assistant's summary against the code.
examples: Tree: app/main.py, app/routes/orders.py, app/db.py, tests/. Search shows 3 of 7 modules import app.db, so the data layer is not isolated behind one module.
Claim: 'all routes check auth.' Searching for the decorator finds it on 4 of 5 routes: the claim is false.

lessons.title: Reading a diff for intent
lessons.objective: Review a diff against its specification in a fixed order and find the changes the specification did not ask for.

concepts.title: Scope creep
concepts.summary: Changes beyond what the specification asked for.

concepts.title: Review order
concepts.summary: Intent and design first, then interfaces, tests, risky paths, then details.

concepts.title: Review comment
concepts.summary: A specific, actionable note tied to a line and a reason.

misconceptions: If the diff looks tidy it is fine; assistants reformat, rename and 'improve' alongside the change.
Review starts at the first line of the diff; start from what the change was supposed to do.
Removing a log line is cosmetic; logs and error handling carry operations behaviour.
sequence: The specification: add an optional limit, default 50, to list_orders.
A diff that also adds ordering and removes a log line.
Review order and what to ask for each unrequested change.
A comment that states the line, the concern and the request.
examples: Diff adds limit=50 (requested), adds ORDER BY created DESC (not requested) and deletes log.info (not requested): 2 changes beyond the spec.

lessons.title: Defects that assistants typically make
lessons.objective: Recognise hallucinated APIs, plausible-but-wrong logic, swallowed errors and tests that were bent to pass.

concepts.title: Hallucinated API
concepts.summary: A call to a function, method or package that does not exist.

concepts.title: Swallowed error
concepts.summary: An exception caught and replaced by a default so the failure disappears.

concepts.title: Off-by-one
concepts.summary: A boundary error of exactly one element.

misconceptions: Code that runs is correct; it can run and return the wrong list.
A hallucinated API always fails loudly; some are real functions with different behaviour from the one assumed.
A passing test suite after an assistant's change shows it fixed the bug; check that tests were not edited to pass.
sequence: A pagination function with 1-indexed pages and a 0-indexed slice.
A try/except that returns 0.
A call to a method that is not in the library.
An assistant that special-cases the failing test input.
examples: items[page*size:(page+1)*size] with page=1, size=10 over range(25) returns 10..19, skipping 0..9.
'abc'.reverse() raises AttributeError because str has no reverse; reversed or slicing [::-1] is the real route.

lessons.title: Security review of generated code
lessons.objective: Find injection, missing authorisation, committed secrets and risky dependencies in a generated change.

concepts.title: SQL injection
concepts.summary: Attacker-controlled text altering the structure of a query.

concepts.title: Broken access control
concepts.summary: A request reaching data its caller should not see.

concepts.title: Dependency risk
concepts.summary: Adding a package that is unmaintained, malicious or non-existent in the registry the name was guessed from.

misconceptions: The assistant knows secure patterns; it reproduces common code, including common insecure code.
Authentication and authorisation are the same; the first asks who you are and the second what you may do.
An import that resolves is safe; a hallucinated name can be registered by an attacker.
sequence: A search endpoint building SQL with an f-string.
The same query parameterised.
An endpoint that returns /orders/{id} without checking the owner.
A new dependency: age, maintainers, name check.
examples: Table users has 4 rows. f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'" with name = x' OR '1'='1 returns all 4 rows; the parameterised form with the same string returns 0.
A key committed to git is exposed even after deletion because history keeps it; rotate it.

lessons.title: Verifying behaviour
lessons.objective: Gather evidence that a change works, and distinguish an assistant's claim from an observed result.

concepts.title: Evidence ladder
concepts.summary: Claim, read code, tests pass, run the feature, check in a realistic environment.

concepts.title: Property
concepts.summary: A statement that must hold for every input, such as the result being a member of the input.

concepts.title: Definition of done
concepts.summary: The evidence you require before merging.

misconceptions: 'All tests pass' is the end of verification; check that the tests exercise the change.
An assistant's report of running the tests is evidence; the log is evidence.
Properties need a framework; a loop over random inputs also tests one.
sequence: A test log: 48 passed, 2 failed, 1 skipped.
my_max returns 0 for all-negative input.
A property: the maximum is an element of the list and is at least every element.
The merge checklist.
examples: 48 + 2 + 1 = 51 tests; 3 are not passing. my_max([-3,-1,-2]) with m = 0 returns 0, which is not in the list.

figures.shows: A test log with counts and a skipped list.
figures.learnerAction: Total the tests and find the skipped ones.

questionPlan.sample: A log reads 48 passed, 2 failed, 1 skipped. How many tests were listed?

questionPlan.answer: The result is an element of the list
choices: The result is an element of the list

lessons.title: Ownership, licensing and privacy
lessons.objective: Decide what may be pasted into an assistant, and who is responsible for licence and data consequences.

concepts.title: Data handling
concepts.summary: What leaves your machine when you prompt, and the vendor's retention and training terms.

concepts.title: Licence risk
concepts.summary: Generated code may reproduce licensed code; the obligation stays with the shipper.

concepts.title: Team policy
concepts.summary: Written rules for which tools, data and repositories are allowed.

misconceptions: If the tool wrote it, I do not need to check its licence; a verbatim reproduction of copyleft code can still bind your project.
Private chats with a tool are private; read the retention and training terms of the plan you are on.
Secrets are safe if deleted from the chat; rotate them.
sequence: Four things you might paste: a stack trace, a customer export, an API key, a public README.
What each exposes.
Where licence questions arise: long verbatim blocks, copied tests, vendored code.
The written policy.
examples: A stack trace with no personal data is usually fine; a customer export and an API key are not, and a pasted key must be rotated.

lessons.title: Working rules and measurement
lessons.objective: Write your own working rules and measure whether AI assistance is helping with delivery metrics rather than output volume.

concepts.title: Change failure rate
concepts.summary: The share of changes that cause a failure needing a fix.

concepts.title: Working rule
concepts.summary: A short statement of when to use the assistant, what to verify and what never to delegate.

concepts.title: Skill atrophy
concepts.summary: Loss of practice in work you stop doing yourself.

misconceptions: More merged changes means more productivity; failures cancel gains.
Speed is the measure; DORA pairs throughput with stability.
The assistant has no downside for learning; skills you never practise fade, so keep some work manual.
sequence: Before and after: 40 merges and 5% failures, then 60 merges and 10%.
Failed and successful merges before and after.
Stability alongside throughput.
A one-page set of rules.
examples: Before: 40 × 0.05 = 2 failed, 38 good. After: 60 × 0.10 = 6 failed, 54 good. Good merges rose (54 − 38)/38 ≈ 42%, while failures tripled.

figures.shows: Merges per month and change failure rate before and after.
